title: City-RAG: Stepping Into a City via Spatially-Grounded Video Generation
claim: Conditioning generation on real-world geo-registered data yields grounded, consistent, controllable long videos where ungrounded generators hallucinate.
layout: Top pipeline strip, then three labeled image-strip rows; green boxes mark starting frames
description: The figure has a top strip and three rows of sample frames. The top strip is a small pipeline. A first street image and a map with a red user-specified trajectory arrow go into a boxed 'City-RAG' module. The module pairs a Street View Database icon (a person and a database cylinder) with a Video Model icon (a neural network). An arrow leads to a stack of generated frames at S. King St, Honolulu. A dashed line separates this from three rows of street-view frames. Row 1 shows London's Westminster Bridge. CityRAG on the left renders Big Ben, and an existing I2V model on the right hallucinates. Row 2 shows a long trajectory with loop closure. Row 3 shows the same Honolulu intersection in snowy and night conditions. Green boxes mark the starting frames, and bold captions sit under each row.
caption: CityRAG generates minutes-long, spatially grounded video sequences that 1) Render real buildings, traffic lights, and roads of a city. From an image taken on the Westminster Bridge in London, CityRAG generates Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament as the viewpoint rotates left, while Veo [ref] hallucinates. 2) Follow a user-defined path and perform loop closure after generating a thousand frames. 3) Are initialized from a first image and respects its weather conditions and dynamic objects. Top: The Westminster Bridge, London. Middle: Calle Quiñones St, San Juan. Bottom: S King St, Honolulu. Starting views are labeled with green bounding boxes.
abstract: We address the problem of generating a 3D-consistent, navigable environment that is spatially grounded: a simulation of a real location. Existing video generative models can produce a plausible sequence that is consistent with a text (T2V) or image (I2V) prompt. However, the capability to reconstruct the real world under arbitrary weather conditions and dynamic object configurations is essential for downstream applications including autonomous driving and robotics simulation. To this end, we present CityRAG, a video generative model that leverages large corpora of geo-registered data as context to ground generation to the physical scene, while maintaining learned priors for complex motion and appearance changes. CityRAG relies on temporally unaligned training data, which teaches the model to semantically disentangle the underlying scene from its transient attributes. Our experiments demonstrate that CityRAG can generate coherent minutes-long, physically grounded video sequences, maintain weather and lighting conditions over thousands of frames, achieve loop closure, and navigate complex trajectories to reconstruct real-world geography.
